I’ve been actively trading this year using my own research and diligence, and someone recommended this app to me. I want to share my experience so others can go in with eyes open.

To be fair, some signals do work. The issue isn’t that everything is wrong. The problem is the options trading signals combined with the community and notification design.

The app sends a constant barrage of notifications showcasing huge percentage gains, paired with very sophisticated, AI-generated messages. It creates a strong impression that these signals are consistently profitable and that “all that glitters is gold.” Over time, that messaging wears down your judgment.

Options trading already requires a very strong mindset and discipline. In this environment, it’s easy to get carried away by FOMO — and I did. As a result, I’ve lost over $15,000 following trades influenced by this app. I fully own my decisions, but the experience felt unsettling: it’s almost uncanny how quickly trades can go south once you act on impulse driven by hype.

When things don’t work out, the app owner points you to help articles and disclaimers, essentially saying “read the content carefully.” But that raises a real question:
If you need that level of caution and filtering, isn’t that exactly what you’d do without the app?

My takeaway:
This app can make trading feel simpler and more certain than it really is. It’s not. Options trading is complex, emotionally taxing, and unforgiving. The presentation of signals here can give a false sense of confidence, especially to retail traders.

I have serious doubts about this app, and I think others should too. If you use it at all, you need extreme restraint, independent verification, and a willingness to ignore most of what you see. Otherwise, the cost can be very real.

View all short term price predictions (and indeed, players) with cynicism. Even, to some degree, the linked article, insofar as it may claim to present a 'master plan' for the hows and whys of market movements.

No external observer has all the pertinent info, and individuals thinking that they (or others they listen to) do reliably have that information, is the general psychological driver that moves a great deal of the money involved in these quasi-casinobanks of the fledgling crypto industry.

If organizations like Bloomberg are going to quote people's price predictions, they should have a way of tracking the accuracy of people's past predictions. Otherwise, this is just noise: of course people holding an instrument want you to believe it will go up. (This isn't crypto-specific; the same applies to equities etc.)
